coding-spend.title: AI spend per employee
coding-spend.note: Approximate sparse read-off from supplied Ramp image; February 2025 technology value $11.87 and final sector values are exact printed labels. Final month is inferred from monthly spacing, approximately July 2026.

omarchy.title: The one-person software team
omarchy.note: All cost, duration, team-size, and total labels transcribed exactly; this is the author’s estimate, not observed billing data.

software-pipeline.title: The software factory
software-pipeline.note: Stage shares and remaining-time labels transcribed exactly. Saved time is original minus remaining. Source labels modest AI as 83% left / 1.20×; AI-pilled 10% left / 10×.

employment.title: Becoming tractor-pilled
employment.note: Approximate decadal read-off of the supplied FT graphic, not an underlying dataset. Agriculture has an additional 1800 point; the other two curves start 1810. Source credits Robert Z Lawrence; S Lebergott (NBER 1966); FRED; BLS.

code-history.title: The market for code, 1980–2025
code-history.note: Modeled annual spending in real 2025 USD. Area components are approximate image read-offs; bubble labels are exact. Original source includes conservative 2040 scenario, despite scene name mentioning history. Bubble area, not radius, represents annual gross LOC.

data.bubbleUnit: Gross lines of code per year

code-future.title: The trillion-dollar agent opportunity
code-future.note: Optimistic modeled annual spending source. Area components are approximate read-offs; $10T and 10T LOC endpoint labels are exact. Conservative variant uses preceding source image, allowing prose to reveal conservative then optimistic outcomes without misleading substitution.

data.bubbleUnit: Gross lines of code per year

solar.title: The solar learning curve
solar.note: Approximate sparse read-offs from supplied OWID image. Both axes logarithmic; capacity in MW, cost per watt in 2019 USD. The source explicitly reports a 20.2% average learning rate and 99.6% price decline since 1976.

experience-curves.title: Cars, solar, and code
experience-curves.note: Approximate sparse read-offs. Source normalizes annual output to starting output; unit costs real 2025 USD. Code uses U.S. software investment as proxy, and 2030 is a dashed scenario. Source endpoint labels exact; values approximate.

productivity.title: Where is the productivity growth?
productivity.note: Approximate plotted-coordinate transcription, labels exact. Latest minus pre-pandemic productivity growth plotted against AI adoption in 2026 H1. Source reports R² = 0.00; mining (NAICS 21) excluded.

tfp.title: Technology and total factor productivity
tfp.note: Totals are exact printed labels; technology components and period boundaries approximate read-offs. Source leaves 1941–1948 as a gap. This is an author-composed technology attribution chart, not direct BLS attribution.

ai-economy.title: AI in the productivity statistics
ai-economy.note: Six source panels faithfully transcribed: two AI impact categories and four historical examples. Values are the source’s claims, not independently verified estimates.

cards.label: Consumer surplus
cards.description: Value reaches people at a near-zero price; GDP under-represents consumer benefit.
examples: Free replacement of software and service purchases
cards.measurement: Little is sold; benefits may escape GDP

cards.label: Producer surplus
cards.description: Value embedded in sold goods and services is transacted and recorded in GDP.

cards.label: Electric lighting
cards.description: Light became ~99.97% cheaper; an hour’s wage buys ~40,000× more. Prices did not record this gain.

cards.label: Free digital goods
cards.description: Free search, encyclopaedias and maps displaced paid services; search alone was worth ~$17.5k/yr/person.

cards.label: Steam
cards.description: Mechanized factories and railways let one worker produce and move far more to market.

cards.label: Automation
cards.description: Programmable machine tools cut labor in every unit, raising output per worker.
